Yes, the story has an appropriate and effective balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The core of the narrative unfolds in vivid, real-time scenes—such as the narrator discovering the half-burned chair, following the couple down Marrow Street in the rising floodwaters, and peering through the gap in their curtains as the woman removes her coat and drinks her tea. These dramatized moments create tension and make the story come alive through concrete sensory details and actions. 

At the same time, the writer skillfully weaves in brief passages of summary and exposition to provide context and compress time where needed. For example, the narrator summarizes the broader setting ("It had been raining for nine days"), offers quick character exposition ("I am a person who returns library books early"), and compresses the aftermath of the flood at the end ("The rain stopped on the twelfth day. People put their ruined furniture out on the curbs..."). This seamless alternation between immediate, dramatized scenes and reflective summary maintains an engaging pace and deepens the emotional resonance of the story without feeling either bogged down or overly dry.
